Local Design Lab · final pressure test

Two columns, four grains, and one shell

Financials became a two-column composition. The Process card was pressure-tested against a family whose two children are at different stages, opened from two different Work Views. And the shell got its subject avatar and 14px of its whitespace back.

Financials 450Process 221 vs 467Shell gap 37 → 23 typecheck rc=0

Financials 60 / 40 1023 × 450

Current Period is the primary financial explanation and takes 60%; Past Due and Payment answer one related question — what needs collecting, and how — and stack in the remaining 40%. The arithmetic is capped at a 380px measure: at full column width a label and its amount drifted apart and the stack stopped reading as a sum.

ActionHomeWhy
Pay nowinside Past DueContextual and primary whenever money is owed
Add charge →under Current Period“Add something that should be billed” is a Current Period intent. Quiet, so it never competes with Pay now
Details →under Current PeriodThe card identity supplies the context
Manage payment →inside PaymentIt owns payers, split, methods, autopay and recovery — so it sits under those facts, not in a footer

There is no separate Manage payers product. Backend semantics do not require one — payers, split and methods are facets of the same configuration.

A future-dated charge is therefore ordinary — a September service date created in August, billable next cycle. Charge type is the platform select sourced from financial_charge_templates, showing configured labels and never keys. Payer targeting offers only what the template permits and resolves against the canonical responsibility model; the command builds no allocation of its own, and allocation math renders only when the split is authoritative.

Ledger GL code: include it

GL code is canonical. lib/financials/gl/ plus accounting/resolveGlMapping.ts and the tables gl_accounts (with code), gl_account_mappings, gl_journal_entries, gl_journal_lines. resolveGlMapping answers exactly the ledger column — which charge category, which mapping key it posts through, which GL account it resolves to, or that it is unmapped. Unmapped renders “— unmapped”, an honest state rather than a blank.

Type labels come from chargeCategoryLabel(). The card renders no raw key and builds no display map — the catalog already owns the vocabulary. Still no running balance.

Mixed grain four renders, one component 221px each

From Tour and from All: identical. Same stage band, same work line, same actions — only the lens chip changes. That is not a convention; it is structural:

Repository proof

buildOperationalContext resolves businessProcess.stageKey from subjectVm.workspace.lifecycle_rail.current_stage_key ?? stage_context.stage_key and contains no reference to a work unit or work view. A lens is structurally incapable of reaching the stage. The only seam it can touch is the stage label fallback (stage_label ?? statusLabel) — never the key. That asymmetry deserves a guard test.

Avery is waitlisted; the case is at Tour; both stay true. Each child's participation projects as supporting context beneath the band, and the scoped child is emphasised, not substituted. A waitlisted child never rewrites the case's stage.

P2 — there is no child-grain Focus Panel, by doctrine

OperationalGrain declares "child" as “Not yet used in the Focus Panel; reserved for child-grain queue row contexts”; a shipped conformance test asserts “grain is always 'case' for Focus Panel contexts”; and operational-grain-doctrine.md §2.4 states the panel “always opens on an Opportunity” and that a child selection is a scope hint which “does not change the Focus Panel's grain.”

So rendering Avery as the subject is a platform change, not a card change. Recommendation: do not build it for this. The scope-hint model answers the operational question, and the doctrine is deliberate.

Two shared owners, top only: the Work-mode scroll container's top padding (py-3 → pt-1 pb-3, −8px) and padding-top on .alloy-os-focus-panel-grid:not(--work), the shared non-Work grid rule (−6px). Sides and bottom keep --alloy-os-fp-pad, so no column width moves and no card's internal spacing changes. No route-specific override.

Caught by measuring, not reading

My first attempt put the rule on .alloy-os-focus-panel-grid--composed — specificity (0,1,0). It silently did nothing, because .alloy-os-focus-panel-grid:not(.alloy-os-focus-panel-grid--work) is (0,2,0) and wins regardless of source order. The rendered paddingTop still read 16px, which is the only reason I noticed.

Subject avatar — one model, generic. The identity block takes personSubjectName / personSubjectImageUrl / personSubjectRecordId and renders CardAvatar — the same primitive the cards use, image with initials fallback — otherwise keeping the household tile, which is right for a family subject. The shell knows a name and perhaps an image; it does not know whether the person is a child, a contact or an employee, so all three work with no per-type code.

No information lost — stage, status, current work, still-needed, due and actions each appear once, and Recent Activity is deliberately dropped. Child divergence is added: the old pair could not express it at all.

H1–H4 — what Enrollment is waiting for

Enrollment's dependency is H2 only. H2 registers four stable collection provider refs — health.allergies, health.conditions, health.medications, health.immunizations — all resolving through one person_health_facts entity with itemEntityType: "person_health_fact" and customer_member_id as the subject context. Four refs and not one, because a Forms group binds to one collection and an operator authoring an allergy section must not receive medications.

H2 guarantees the refs are stable, the item entity type is fixed, and a binding authored before any data exists resolves to an empty collection, never an error. Forms binding and Trust proposals both start working at H2 — adaptFormSubmissionToRelatedRecordProposals stops emitting unknown_provider and starts emitting valid.

M1 must land before H2, or the health grain and the provider's sourceEntityType disagree from day one.
